extracted.intended_audience: literate general public; writers, journalists, and public officials (mid-18th-century readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and editorial guidance embedded in an 18th‑century essay about newspapers, public honours, and monument inscriptions — advising how news should be gathered and presented, how to plan serialized coverage, and how to compose public inscriptions so they remain clear to posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper_selection_and_compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: The compilation of newspapers is often committed to narrow and mercenary minds, who are content to fill their paper with whatever matter, without industry to gather, or discernment to select.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters should exercise industry in gathering material and discernment in selecting what to publish; avoid letting mercenary motives drive content choices. The essay criticises cheap multiplication of journals that do not increase knowledge and suggests that reporting requires effort and judgement rather than mere filling of space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_repetition_and_premature_reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The tale of the morning paper is told again in the evening, and the narratives of the evening are bought again in the morning. These repetitions waste time, but they do not shorten it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify reports before publishing to avoid premature or contradictory accounts. Repetition across issues tires readers and reduces value. The Bull-dog/Friseur example is used to show how successive premature or contradicted reports across morning/evening papers create confusion and fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial_planning_and_serialisation_for_reader_engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The morning and evening authors might divide an event between them; a single action ... might be gradually discovered, so as to vary a whole week with joy, anxiety, and conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors can deliberately plan coverage — staggering details and developments across issues — to sustain reader interest. Thoughtful division of material among issues (or writers) creates variety and engagement, rather than everybody echoing the same summary at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth_over_surface_fascination_in_news
rubrics_metrics.description: This universal diffusion of instruction ... fills the nation with superficial disputants; enables those to talk who were born to work; and affords information sufficient to elate vanity, and stiffen obstinacy, but too little to enlarge the mind into complete skill for full comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for reporting that enlarges understanding rather than just supplies tidbits that flatter vanity. Prefer informative, thoughtfully selected material that fosters deeper comprehension rather than merely servicing gossip, sensation, or shallow disputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision_and_clarity_in_public_inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The pedestal should be inscribed with a concise account of this great performance. The composition of this narrative ought not to be committed rashly to improper hands. ... danger lest they admit some phrases which, though well understood at present, may be ambiguous in another century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose public inscriptions (and analogous commemorative texts) with brevity and extreme care: use clear, unambiguous wording that will survive shifts in language or custom. Avoid idioms or constructions that could be misread by later readers; state essential facts and motives explicitly (example: record that 'she won her wager' to prevent future misinterpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make_rewards_meaningful_and_context-appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves and flowers are transitory things; profit is the end of honour; and the event of every undertaking only by the money that is gained or lost. To strew the road with daisies and lilies, is to mock merit, and delude hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rewarding public feats, choose recognitions that have real, contemporary value to the recipient and will properly signal worth to others. Symbolic tokens that lack practical value (flowers) may be seen as inadequate or mocking; consider monetary awards or durable honours (statues, inscriptions) when the aim is meaningful recompense and public emulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_contemporary_phraseology_likely_to_confuse_posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rhetoricians of Newmarket ... should undertake to express it, there is danger lest they admit some phrases which, though well understood at present, may be ambiguous in another century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming texts at posterity — inscriptions, monuments, official records — avoid fashionable or transient phrasing. Prefer timeless, literal formulations and include clarifying details (who did what and why) so future readers cannot reasonably misconstrue the facts or motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_graded_simulation_and_exposure_in_training
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a fortification be raised on Salisbury Plain, ... let the inclosure be filled with beef and ale ... lead them in exact order ... Contrive that they may approach the place fasting about an hour after dinner-time, assure them that there is no danger, and command an attack. ... vary its appearance ... a cook may throw fat upon the fire ... sometimes, by the clatter of empty pots, they may be inured to formidable noises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical training (the essay uses a military example), employ staged, progressively challenging simulations that habituate participants to sights, smells, and sounds of the real situation. Use graded increases in stressors and varied scenarios so trainees learn to face fear and act under adverse sensory conditions. (Though military in subject, the method is a general recommendation for experiential training design.)
